archetype.name: Playoff Team (pass-first)
archetype.definition: A Burrow-led offense that throws more than anyone, now paired with a pass rush that leads the league in sacks: good enough by efficiency to be a real AFC threat, with a defense that still has to prove it holds up.

report.headline: Burrow's arm and a league-best sack total have the Bengals playing like contenders.
report.take:
Cincinnati is 4-2, but the efficiency says the record is, if anything, slightly modest. Net EPA ranks 3rd, the point differential is 4th, and wins over expected sits at a near-neutral 0.4, so this isn't a team living on close-game luck. The identity is unmistakable: the Bengals pass 7.4 points more often than the situation calls for, the most in the league, and with Burrow starting every game the pass offense ranks 6th in EPA. The run game is a support act. A 3.6-yard average ranks 23rd, but the line ranks 4th in stuff rate and 3rd in short-yardage conversion, so it's less a broken run game than one that rarely breaks anything long.

The real story is the defense, because history says it shouldn't be this good. Last year's unit ranked 29th in EPA allowed and gave up 28.9 points a game; the year before it was 27th. This year it's 11th overall and 5th against the pass, driven by a rush with 21 sacks (1st) and a 2nd-ranked sack rate. It's also a deep-ball defense, 4th in deep EPA allowed, and it tightens in the red zone (3rd in TD rate allowed).

What the averages hide is how that defense gives up ground. It's 30th in EPA allowed on short passes, 29th in missed tackle rate and 30th on third down. Opponents march, extend drives and pile up yardage (21st in yards allowed) before the sacks and red-zone stands bail it out. Takeaways have also been lumpy: four against Tampa and three against Miami rescued games where the offense or run defense struggled. A defense that depends on sacks and goal-line stops to offset bad tackling is more fragile than one that simply gets off the field.

The arc is upward. The two losses came with two turnovers apiece, and the Jacksonville game added 108 penalty yards and a 23-yard rushing day. Since then the passing game has produced 13.9 and 18.2 EPA, and the Baltimore rout came with only 15 penalty yards. If Burrow stays upright, this offense travels; the question for January is whether the improved defense is a new baseline or a hot six weeks.

strengths.title: League's most aggressive passing attack
strengths.body: No offense leans on the pass more relative to situation, and it pays: pass EPA ranks 6th and overall success rate 6th. Higgins and Chase split the volume almost evenly, so coverage can't tilt to one side. With a healthy Burrow and a 7th-ranked sack rate allowed, this is the most sustainable part of the profile.

strengths.title: A pass rush that finishes
strengths.body: Pressure rate is only 10th, but the conversion of pressure into sacks is elite, and it shows up in nearly every box score, with four sacks in four of six games. Finishing rate tends to drift toward pressure rate over a season, so expect the sack pace to cool a bit, but the rush is real.

strengths.title: Nothing over the top, little in the red zone
strengths.body: The secondary takes away the deep ball and the defense stiffens inside the 20, which is why points allowed rank 8th despite poor yardage numbers. Red-zone rates are noisy over six games, so this part is the likeliest to give back some ground.

concerns.title: Underneath leaks and missed tackles
concerns.body: The flip side of protecting deep is giving up the short game, and poor tackling turns completions into first downs. That's why third down ranks 30th and the defense spends long stretches on the field. It's a structural flaw, not noise, and good short-passing teams like Kansas City and Pittsburgh down the stretch will test it.

concerns.title: Defensive history argues for caution
concerns.body: This unit ranked 29th and 27th in EPA allowed the last two seasons. Six good weeks against a mix of offenses is encouraging, but bend-don't-break defenses that rely on sacks and red-zone stops tend to regress toward their yardage numbers.

concerns.title: Run game can vanish
concerns.body: The ground game converts short yardage but rarely gains chunks, and when it disappeared against Jacksonville the offense turned one-dimensional. With the pass this good, it's a cost of the identity rather than a crisis, but it limits the ability to close games.

trend.note: After a 2-2 start where turnovers and penalties cost two games, the passing game has taken over, posting 13.9 and 18.2 EPA in wins at Miami and Baltimore, the second a 22-point rout in the division.

nextGame.headline: A struggling Titans offense visits a team built to bury it
nextGame.body:
Tennessee arrives 1-6 with the league's 31st-ranked offense by EPA and last in yards per game, and it plays slow, run-leaning football (30th in pass rate over expected). Its defense is the soft spot Cincinnati wants: 24th against the pass, 26th in explosive pass rate allowed, and especially generous to opposing WR1s. The Titans tackle well and keep their QB clean, so this won't be a sack party by default, but the Bengals' passing game should find room. The Book has Cincinnati at -10 with a 46.5 total.

Availability tilts further toward Cincinnati. The Titans are without receiver Calvin Ridley and back Tyjae Spears, thinning an already weak offense, and their punter is questionable. For the Bengals, safety Kyle Dugger is out, a limited-snap loss, while the tight end room is thin with Tanner Hudson on IR and Erick All Jr. questionable after leaving the Baltimore game with a knee injury.

waysToWin.title: Feed the WR1 against a leaky secondary
waysToWin.body: Tennessee has let opposing WR1s score well above their usual output and ranks poorly in EPA allowed to them. Higgins leads the team in targets, and with Chase alongside him the Titans can't bracket both. An early two-score lead forces a run-first offense out of its comfort zone.

waysToWin.title: Make Cam Ward play from behind
waysToWin.body: The Titans' offense ranks near the bottom passing and wants to run. Once they're forced to throw, Cincinnati's league-leading sack unit gets obvious passing downs, even against a line that has limited hits on its QB.

waysToLose.title: Short-game drives and fourth-down gambles
waysToLose.body: Tennessee goes for it on fourth down more than anyone, and Cincinnati is 30th on third down and against short passes. If the Titans string together long, clock-eating drives and convert in the gray zone, a big favorite can find itself in a one-score fourth quarter.

waysToLose.title: Giving the ball away again
waysToLose.body: Both losses came with two turnovers and the Jacksonville loss also brought 108 penalty yards. Short fields are the only realistic way this Titans offense scores enough to win.

nextGame.watch: Whether Tennessee's run game can stay on schedule against a Bengals front that ranks 25th in explosive runs allowed; if not, the pass rush takes over.

restOfSeason.body:
The offense is the bankable piece: an elite, pass-heavy attack with a healthy Burrow and a line that limits sacks has a history of producing points in Cincinnati, and the 2024 offense ranked 7th in EPA too. Expect scoring to stay in the upper tier. The defense is where regression lives. The sack finishing rate, red-zone stops and spiky takeaways all tend to drift back, while the missed tackles and third-down leaks are structural, so points allowed should rise somewhat from the current pace.

The schedule splits sharply. Washington, New Orleans and Indianapolis are soft, but four division games remain against Pittsburgh, Cleveland twice and Baltimore, plus Kansas City, with Pittsburgh, Cleveland and Kansas City all owning top-seven defenses. In a tight AFC North, the title likely comes down to those games; the efficiency says this is the most complete team in the division.
swingFactors: Burrow's health behind a line allowing frequent hits
Whether the defense keeps winning in the red zone
Six division and Kansas City games against top defenses

confidence.note: Six games, stable QB and a proven offense, but a defense outrunning its recent history.
